thread.title_full: Maximize your tax return with these Hawaiʻi tax credits - NewsBreak

author: Cameron Macedonio
title: Maximize your tax return with these Hawaiʻi tax credits - NewsBreak
text:
By Cameron Macedonio ,
6 hours ago
HONOLULU (KHON2) — As tax season is in full swing, Hawaiʻi’s taxpayers should be looking for ways to maximize their tax refunds so they can get as much money back as possible.
While filling out your Form 1040 and calling it a day may be the easiest way to handle the tax paperwork headaches, you may be missing out on hundreds — if not thousands — of potential tax credits.
The Hawaiʻi Department of Taxation has multiple forms for common circumstances that taxpayers can fill out and submit in order to get back the money you deserve.
However, there is no one-size-fits-all solution to your taxes. Tax credit and deduction amounts can vary based on factors like income, number of dependents and other unique information. For advice tailored to your specific financial situation, consult a tax professional.
Hiring a professional tax preparer or do it yourself? The BBB got the details If you already filed your taxes, no need to worry — you can still work to get more tax credit. Many credits are able to claim up to 12 months after the close of the tax year, the Department of Taxation said. For specific information, check on your specific form.
Schedule X The Schedule X form is a two-in-one form that allows taxpayers to deduct living and childcare expenses from their taxes. If you don’t have dependents but can deduct living expenses, that’s possible to do too — you don’t need to qualify for both credits to fill out the form.
Part one of the form is credit for low-income renters. If your adjusted gross income is less than $30,000, you may be able to get credit for the amount of rent you paid in 2025.
The remainder of the form is to get credit for child and dependent care costs. If you have at least one qualified dependent, are employed or looking for a job and paid for services or expenses for your dependent, you can get credit on your taxes.
According to the Department of Taxation, you can get up to $10,000 credit in eligible expenses if you have one dependent or up to $20,000 credit in eligible expenses if you have two or more dependents.
Schedule X can be downloaded and viewed online .
Which tax bracket are you in, and how much is the standard deduction? Form N-311 Those looking to maximize their tax credits should also look at Form N-311, or the Hawaiʻi Food/Excise Tax Credit.
Based on your Federal Adjusted Gross Income and other factors, you could get up to $1,100 in credit if eligible.
To qualify for the credit, you must be physically present in Hawaiʻi for more than nine months throughout the tax year, not claimed as a dependent and not be incarcerated.
If filing as a single individual, your Federal Adjusted Gross Income must not be more than $40,000 to qualify for the credit. For all other filing statuses, the combined Federal Adjusted Gross Income must not exceed $60,000.
Form N-311 can be downloaded and viewed online .
6 things to know to access Hawaiʻi’s free tax prep service Form N-139 Those who moved to, within or from Hawaiʻi for work are able to get credit for their moving expenses such as temporary lodging costs, flights and other “reasonable expenses.”
Taxpayers looking to get credit for their move must pass two different eligibility tests in order to qualify: the distance test and the time test.
For distance, your new workplace must be at least 50 miles further from your old home than your old job. For time, you must work full time in the area of your new workplace for at least 39 weeks after your move.
There are multiple exceptions based on disability, other economic factors and employment status, which can be found on the form’s instructions.
Additionally, reimbursed moving expenses from your company are not creditable.
Form N-139 can be downloaded and viewed online .
For a complete list of individual tax forms that can supplement your tax credit, visit the Department of Taxation’s website .
